claim: The Escherichia coli GroE chaperonin system comprises GroEL and its co-factor GroES.
source: The Escherichia coli GroE chaperonin system, which comprises GroEL and its co-factor GroES, assists protein folding in vivo and in vitro in an ATP-dependent manner (Thirumalai and Lorimer, 2001; Saibil et al., 2013; Hayer-Hartl et al., 2016; Gruber and Horovitz, 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The GroE chaperonin system assists protein folding in vivo and in vitro in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: The Escherichia coli GroE chaperonin system, which comprises GroEL and its co-factor GroES, assists protein folding in vivo and in vitro in an ATP-dependent manner (Thirumalai and Lorimer, 2001; Saibil et al., 2013; Hayer-Hartl et al., 2016; Gruber and Horovitz, 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Binding of GroES to GroEL forms a cage in which encapsulated substrate proteins can fold in isolation from bulk solution.
source: Binding of GroES to GroEL forms a cage in which encapsulated substrate proteins can fold in isolation from bulk solution.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structural and functional consequence of GroES binding to GroEL.

claim: It is unclear whether the GroE cavity is a 'passive cage' in which protein substrate aggregation is prevented but the folding pathway is unchanged or a chamber in which the folding process is altered.
source: The GroE system has been studied intensively for more than three decades, but it is still unclear and controversial whether its cavity is a 'passive cage' in which protein substrate aggregation is prevented but the folding pathway is unchanged or a chamber in which the folding process is altered in some manner.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an unresolved question in the field.

claim: It is unclear whether encapsulation in the GroE cavity is thermodynamically stabilizing or destabilizing.
source: It is also unclear whether encapsulation in the GroE cavity is thermodynamically stabilizing, for example because of confinement, or destabilizing owing, for example, to a diminished hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an open question regarding the thermodynamic effects of encapsulation.

claim: According to some studies, encapsulation prevents aggregation but does not alter the protein substrate's folding pathway and kinetics.
source: According to some studies, encapsulation prevents aggregation but does not alter the protein substrate's folding pathway and kinetics (Horst et al., 2007; Tyagi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Encapsulation retards the folding of rhodanese's C-terminal domain but has no effect on its N-terminal domain.
source: In the case of rhodanese, for example, it was reported that encapsulation retards the folding of its C-terminal domain but has no effect on its N-terminal domain (Hofmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: GroEL repairs a folding defect of a mutant of maltose-binding protein by accelerating the formation of an on-pathway intermediate.
source: Recent work showed, for example, that GroEL repairs a folding defect of a mutant of maltose-binding protein by accelerating the formation of an on-pathway intermediate (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: Accelerated folding upon encapsulation has been attributed to steric confinement and the negative charges of the cavity walls.
source: Accelerated folding upon encapsulation has been attributed to steric confinement and the negative charges of the cavity walls (Tang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from a cited study.

claim: Accelerated folding upon encapsulation has been attributed to substrate interactions with the cavity-protruding C-terminal tails of GroEL, which comprise Gly-Gly-Met repeats.
source: It has also been attributed to substrate interactions with the cavity-protruding C-terminal tails of GroEL, which comprise Gly-Gly-Met repeats (Tang et al., 2006; Weaver and Rye, 2014; Weaver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cavity-confined water can enhance the hydrophobic effect by accumulating near the cavity walls.
source: In addition, GroEL-mediated folding can be affected by the cavity-confined water, which can enhance the hydrophobic effect (and thus accelerate folding) by accumulating near the cavity walls (England et al., 2008) or diminish it (and thus slow folding) by being more ordered.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from a cited study.

claim: Cavity-confined water can diminish the hydrophobic effect by being more ordered.
source: In addition, GroEL-mediated folding can be affected by the cavity-confined water, which can enhance the hydrophobic effect (and thus accelerate folding) by accumulating near the cavity walls (England et al., 2008) or diminish it (and thus slow folding) by being more ordered.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the discussion of water structure effects.

claim: According to the iterative annealing model, encapsulated misfolded protein substrates undergo ATP-promoted forced-unfolding.
source: Finally, an even more 'active' mechanism has been proposed according to which encapsulated misfolded protein substrates undergo ATP-promoted forced-unfolding (Weaver and Rye, 2014), in accordance with the iterative annealing model (Todd et al., 1996), thereby giving them further opportunity to fold correctly.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by citations.

claim: The iterative annealing model predicts higher folding yields.
source: The iterative annealing model predicts higher folding yields but it has been suggested that annealing can also lead to accelerated folding (Tang et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2014; Weaver and Rye, 2014; Weaver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction of the iterative annealing model supported by citations.

claim: Annealing can lead to accelerated folding.
source: The iterative annealing model predicts higher folding yields but it has been suggested that annealing can also lead to accelerated folding (Tang et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2014; Weaver and Rye, 2014; Weaver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion from cited studies.

claim: Protein substrates spend variable amounts of time folding in the cavity and in bulk solution because of GroEL-GroES cycling and the leakiness of its cavity.
source: One complication in understanding the thermodynamic effects of encapsulation has been that protein substrates spend variable amounts of time folding in the cavity and in bulk solution because of GroEL-GroES cycling and the leakiness of its cavity (Motojima and Yoshida, 2010).
evidence: This is a complication noted in the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The complex of single-ring GroEL with GroES has been suggested to form during GroEL's normal reaction cycle.
source: As shown below, such leakiness is even greater in the complex of single-ring GroEL with GroES, which was used in some studies (Hofmann et al., 2010) and has been suggested to form during GroEL's normal reaction cycle (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion from a cited study.

claim: A chimera of dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda (DHFRMp) fused to eGFP is encapsulated in the BeFx-stabilized GroEL-GroES2 complex.
source: An appropriate system was found to be a chimera of dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda (DHFRMp) fused to eGFP, which is encapsulated in the football-shaped and non-cycling BeFx-stabilized GroEL-GroES2 complex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Protein stability in the GroEL cavity is reduced dramatically in comparison with bulk solution.
source: Our results show that protein stability in the GroEL cavity is reduced dramatically in comparison with bulk solution.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cavity volume of the GroEL-GroES2 complex is about 175,000 Å3.
source: The cavity volume is about 175,000 Å3 whereas that of the chimera (which is not drawn to scale) is about 58,000 Å3 assuming 1.23 Å3 per Da.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: The volume of the DHFRMp-eGFP chimera is about 58,000 Å3 assuming 1.23 Å3 per Da.
source: The cavity volume is about 175,000 Å3 whereas that of the chimera (which is not drawn to scale) is about 58,000 Å3 assuming 1.23 Å3 per Da.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and calculated based on a standard conversion factor.

claim: eGFP-containing 'football' complexes remain intact and eGFP does not escape during overnight incubation at room temperature.
source: Taken together, these results show that the GroEL-GroES2 football-shaped complexes remained intact and that eGFP did not escape outside during the overnight incubation.
evidence: This is concluded from gel-filtration and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the eGFP escaped from the cavity of the complex of single-ring GroEL with GroES after overnight incubation at room temperature.
source: Most of the eGFP was found in fractions (peak 3) that contain no GroEL and GroES (inset), thereby indicating that eGFP escaped from the cavity of the complex of SR1 with GroES.
evidence: This is concluded from gel-filtration and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda is a relatively unstable protein at room temperature.
source: We chose to use dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda, a psychrophilic bacterium with an optimal growth temperature at 2°C, as a model substrate since it is a relatively unstable protein at room temperature Xu et al., 2003 whose folding can be monitored easily by measuring the regain in enzyme activity.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: Moritella profunda is a psychrophilic bacterium with an optimal growth temperature at 2°C.
source: We chose to use dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda, a psychrophilic bacterium with an optimal growth temperature at 2°C, as a model substrate since it is a relatively unstable protein at room temperature Xu et al., 2003 whose folding can be monitored easily by measuring the regain in enzyme activity.
evidence: This is stated directly as background information.

claim: DHFRMp folding can be monitored easily by measuring the regain in enzyme activity.
source: We chose to use dihydrofolate reductase from Moritella profunda, a psychrophilic bacterium with an optimal growth temperature at 2°C, as a model substrate since it is a relatively unstable protein at room temperature Xu et al., 2003 whose folding can be monitored easily by measuring the regain in enzyme activity.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for choosing this protein.

claim: DHFRMp was fused to the C-terminus of eGFP in order to further destabilize it.
source: DHFRMp was fused to the C-terminus of enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) in order to further destabilize it as observed before for other proteins (Sokolovski et al., 2015; Dave et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a design rationale supported by citations.

claim: The fusion to eGFP facilitated easy and sensitive determination of the location of the substrate.
source: The fusion to eGFP also facilitated easy and sensitive determination of the location of the substrate, that is whether it is in the cavity or has leaked outside of it.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage of the fusion design.

claim: The apparent melting temperature of DHFRMp alone in bulk solution is about 41.2 (±1.8) °C.
source: Under our conditions, the apparent melting temperature, Tm, in bulk solution of DHFRMp alone was found to be about 41.2 (±1.8) °C whereas DHFRMp fused to eGFP was found to be strongly destabilized with a Tm of 22.8 (±1.1) °C (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a measured value reported in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: DHFRMp fused to eGFP is strongly destabilized with a Tm of 22.8 (±1.1) °C in bulk solution.
source: Under our conditions, the apparent melting temperature, Tm, in bulk solution of DHFRMp alone was found to be about 41.2 (±1.8) °C whereas DHFRMp fused to eGFP was found to be strongly destabilized with a Tm of 22.8 (±1.1) °C (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a measured value reported in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: eGFP in the chimera is destabilized in bulk solution relative to eGFP alone, with Tm values of 76.3 (±0.3) and 81.3 (±1.3) °C, respectively.
source: eGFP in the chimera was also found to be destabilized in bulk solution relative to eGFP alone, but to a lesser extent, with Tm values of 76.3 (±0.3) and 81.3 (±1.3) °C, respectively.
evidence: This is a measured comparison reported in the text.

claim: The BeFx-stabilized GroEL-GroES2 'football' complex is stabilized in the presence of BeFx.
source: It has been reported that the GroEL-GroES2 complex is stabilized in the presence of BeFx (Taguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claim: A lag phase is observed in the DHFR activity of the encapsulated chimera but not the free chimera.
source: The data show a lag phase followed by a linear phase (Figure 3) before activity starts to diminish owing to substrate depletion. Strikingly, the lag phase is absent when the chimera is free in bulk solution (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rate constant associated with the lag phase decreases with increasing substrate concentrations for the encapsulated chimera.
source: Inspection of Equation 2 shows that the value of the observed rate constant, λ, decreases with increasing substrate concentration as observed here in the case of the encapsulated chimera (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The DHFRMp part of the chimera is significantly destabilized in the cavity, but not in bulk solution.
source: This finding indicates that the DHFRMp part of the chimera is significantly destabilized in the cavity, but not in bulk solution (where the lag phase is absent), and that the substrates DHF and NADPH shift its equilibrium toward the folded state via a conformational selection mechanism.
evidence: This is concluded from the kinetic data showing substrate concentration dependence.

claim: The substrates DHF and NADPH shift the equilibrium of the DHFRMp part of the chimera toward the folded state via a conformational selection mechanism.
source: This finding indicates that the DHFRMp part of the chimera is significantly destabilized in the cavity, but not in bulk solution (where the lag phase is absent), and that the substrates DHF and NADPH shift its equilibrium toward the folded state via a conformational selection mechanism.
evidence: This is concluded from the kinetic data showing substrate concentration dependence.

claim: Both DHF and NADPH stabilize the DHFRMp part of the chimera in bulk solution.
source: In agreement with this finding, temperature melts of the chimera in bulk solution show that both DHF and NADPH stabilize its DHFRMp part (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the temperature melt data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 20% of human DHFR mis-folds inside the cavity of the non-cycling complex of single-ring GroEL with GroES.
source: This possibility is unlikely, however, because it was found that only 20% of human DHFR mis-folds inside the cavity of the non-cycling complex of single-ring GroEL with GroES (Horst et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study used to support an argument.

claim: The folding rate constant of the DHFRMp part of the chimera inside the cavity is 1.4 (±0.4) x 10−4 sec−1.
source: Values of the folding and unfolding rate constants were obtained by fitting the plot of λ as a function of substrate (DHF) concentration to Equation 2 and found to be 1.4 (±0.4) x 10−4 and 7.3 (±0.8) x 10−3 sec, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a measured value obtained from fitting experimental data.

claim: The unfolding rate constant of the DHFRMp part of the chimera inside the cavity is 7.3 (±0.8) x 10−3 sec−1.
source: Values of the folding and unfolding rate constants were obtained by fitting the plot of λ as a function of substrate (DHF) concentration to Equation 2 and found to be 1.4 (±0.4) x 10−4 and 7.3 (±0.8) x 10−3 sec, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a measured value obtained from fitting experimental data.

claim: The stability of the cavity-confined fused DHFRMp, in the absence of the substrates DHF and NADPH, is 2.4 (±0.2) kcal mol−1.
source: Consequently, the stability of the cavity-confined fused DHFRMp, in the absence of the substrates DHF and NADPH, is 2.4 (±0.2) kcal mol−1, that is the folded state is extremely destabilized so that it is less stable than the unfolded state.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured folding and unfolding rate constants.

claim: The folded state of cavity-confined fused DHFRMp is extremely destabilized so that it is less stable than the unfolded state.
source: Consequently, the stability of the cavity-confined fused DHFRMp, in the absence of the substrates DHF and NADPH, is 2.4 (±0.2) kcal mol−1, that is the folded state is extremely destabilized so that it is less stable than the unfolded state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the positive free energy value.

claim: The stability in bulk solution of fused DHFRMp, in the absence of the substrates DHF and NADPH, is −3.45 (±0.09) kcal mol−1.
source: By contrast, the stability in bulk solution of fused DHFRMp, in the absence of the substrates DHF and NADPH, is −3.45 (±0.09) kcal mol−1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measured value obtained from GuHCl denaturation experiments.

claim: Encapsulation in the GroEL cavity destabilizes the DHFRMp part of the chimera by more than five kcal mol−1 relative to bulk solution.
source: Taken together, the results obtained here show that encapsulation in the GroEL cavity destabilizes the DHFRMp part of the chimera by more than five kcal mol−1 relative to bulk solution.
evidence: This is calculated from the difference in stability values between caged and free protein.

claim: The Km value of the encapsulated fused DHFRMp for DHF is about 0.28 (±0.09) mM.
source: The Km value of the encapsulated fused DHFRMp for DHF is about 0.28 (±0.09) mM and, thus, about 10-fold higher than the value of 33 (±2) µM measured in bulk solution (Figure 4C), in agreement with a previous determination (Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a measured value from enzyme kinetics experiments.

claim: The Km value of the free fused DHFRMp for DHF is 33 (±2) µM in bulk solution.
source: The Km value of the encapsulated fused DHFRMp for DHF is about 0.28 (±0.09) mM and, thus, about 10-fold higher than the value of 33 (±2) µM measured in bulk solution (Figure 4C), in agreement with a previous determination (Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a measured value from enzyme kinetics experiments.

claim: The Km value of encapsulated fused DHFRMp is about 10-fold higher than that in bulk solution.
source: The Km value of the encapsulated fused DHFRMp for DHF is about 0.28 (±0.09) mM and, thus, about 10-fold higher than the value of 33 (±2) µM measured in bulk solution (Figure 4C), in agreement with a previous determination (Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured Km values.

claim: The rotational time of the free chimera is 22.85 (±0.30) ns.
source: Fits of the decay curves for the free and caged chimeras yielded similar rotational times of 22.85 (±0.30) ns and 25.40 (±0.45) ns, respectively (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy decay experiments.

claim: The rotational time of the caged chimera is 25.40 (±0.45) ns.
source: Fits of the decay curves for the free and caged chimeras yielded similar rotational times of 22.85 (±0.30) ns and 25.40 (±0.45) ns, respectively (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy decay experiments.

claim: The rotational time of free eGFP is 14.38 (±0.20) ns.
source: Likewise, the fits of the decay curves for free and caged eGFPs yielded similar rotational times of 14.38 (±0.20) ns and 15.90 (±0.25) ns, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), in agreement with previous work (Striker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy decay experiments.

claim: The rotational time of caged eGFP is 15.90 (±0.25) ns.
source: Likewise, the fits of the decay curves for free and caged eGFPs yielded similar rotational times of 14.38 (±0.20) ns and 15.90 (±0.25) ns, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), in agreement with previous work (Striker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy decay experiments.

claim: The results indicate free mobility of the chimera inside the GroEL football complex.
source: The results indicate free mobility of the chimera and eGFP inside the GroEL football complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the similar rotational times of free and caged proteins.

claim: It is unlikely that the cavity-induced thermodynamic destabilization of the fused DHFRMp is due to interactions with the cavity walls.
source: It is, therefore, unlikely that the cavity-induced thermodynamic destabilization of the fused DHFRMp is due to interactions with the cavity walls.
evidence: This is concluded from the fluorescence anisotropy data showing free mobility.

claim: Protein stability in the chaperonin cage is reduced dramatically by more than 5 kcal mol−1 compared to that in bulk solution.
source: Our results show that protein stability in the chaperonin cage is reduced dramatically by more than 5 kcal mol−1 compared to that in bulk solution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Steric confinement alone is expected to be stabilizing.
source: Given that steric confinement alone is expected to be stabilizing, our results indicate that protein destabilization in the cavity is likely to be due to hydrophobic and/or electrostatic effects.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Protein destabilization in the cavity is likely to be due to hydrophobic and/or electrostatic effects.
source: Given that steric confinement alone is expected to be stabilizing, our results indicate that protein destabilization in the cavity is likely to be due to hydrophobic and/or electrostatic effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that destabilization occurs despite confinement being stabilizing.

claim: Water in the cavity may become more ordered in the presence of a substrate protein, thereby leading to a diminished hydrophobic effect.
source: One possibility is that water in the cavity becomes more ordered in the presence of a substrate protein, thereby leading to a diminished hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism for the observed destabilization.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations have shown that pairwise hydrophobic interactions are destabilized in hydrophobic nanopores when they contain water at bulk density.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations have shown that pairwise hydrophobic interactions are destabilized in hydrophobic nanopores when they contain water at bulk density (Vaitheeswaran and Thirumalai, 2008), as indicated by some evidence in the case of the GroEL cavity (Franck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from cited simulation studies.

claim: There is some evidence that the GroEL cavity contains water at bulk density.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations have shown that pairwise hydrophobic interactions are destabilized in hydrophobic nanopores when they contain water at bulk density (Vaitheeswaran and Thirumalai, 2008), as indicated by some evidence in the case of the GroEL cavity (Franck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is indicated by a cited study.

claim: The cavity walls of the 'football' complexes are charged.
source: The cavity walls of the 'football' complexes in our experiments are, however, charged and the extent of destabilization would, therefore, depend on many factors including the distribution of charges on the cavity walls, the cavity geometry and the presence of regions where the water structure is disrupted.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the experimental system.

claim: Substrate proteins first bind to GroEL in its apo state and can become destabilized through binding to its hydrophobic cavity walls.
source: Substrate proteins first bind to GroEL in its apo state and can become destabilized through binding to its hydrophobic cavity walls (see, for example, Libich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as part of the GroEL mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: ATP binding to the GroEL-protein substrate complex can cause further unfolding due to a stretching force applied to the substrate protein upon ATP-binding-promoted conformational changes.
source: ATP binding to the GroEL-protein substrate complex, which follows, can cause further unfolding due to a stretching force applied to the substrate protein upon ATP-binding-promoted conformational changes (Weaver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as part of the GroEL mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: Protein substrates are encapsulated in the GroES-capped cavity for 1–10 s before being discharged into bulk solution.
source: Next, protein substrates are encapsulated in the GroES-capped cavity for 1–10 s (Bigman and Horovitz, 2019) before being discharged into bulk solution.
evidence: This is stated as part of the GroEL mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: The magnitude and possibly direction of the encapsulation effect is likely to depend on the protein substrate's size and other properties.
source: It is important to point out, however, that the magnitude (and possibly direction) of the effect is likely to depend on the protein substrate's size and other properties.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat to the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The finding that the cavity environment is destabilizing supports the iterative annealing mechanism of action proposed for the chaperonin GroEL.
source: Finally, it is important to note that our finding that the cavity environment is destabilizing supports the iterative annealing mechanism of action proposed for the chaperonin GroEL (Todd et al., 1996; Thirumalai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: According to the iterative annealing mechanism, protein substrates undergo kinetic partitioning, during each reaction cycle of GroEL, between productive folding to the native state and mis-folding.
source: According to this mechanism, protein substrates undergo kinetic partitioning, during each reaction cycle of GroEL, between productive folding to the native state and mis-folding.
evidence: This is a description of the iterative annealing mechanism.

claim: The remaining fraction of mis-folded protein substrates are rebound to GroEL and (partially) unfolded, thereby giving them new opportunity to fold correctly.
source: The remaining fraction of mis-folded protein substrates are then rebound to GroEL and (partially) unfolded, thereby giving them new opportunity to fold correctly.
evidence: This is a description of the iterative annealing mechanism.

claim: (Partial) unfolding is achieved not only because of binding to the hydrophobic cavity of the apo state and ATP-promoted forced unfolding, but also because it is strongly favored thermodynamically under the conditions in the GroES-capped cavity.
source: Our results show that (partial) unfolding is achieved not only because of binding to the hydrophobic cavity of the apo state and ATP-promoted forced unfolding, as shown before by others, but also because it is strongly favored thermodynamically under the conditions in the GroES-capped cavity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion integrating the current findings with previous work.

claim: The melting temperature of the DHFRMp part of the chimera increases by about 8°C in the presence of NADPH.
source: Under the conditions here, the melting temperature of the DHFRMp part of the chimera increases, in the presence of NADPH and DHF, by about 8°C and 31°C, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The melting temperature of the DHFRMp part of the chimera increases by about 31°C in the presence of DHF.
source: Under the conditions here, the melting temperature of the DHFRMp part of the chimera increases, in the presence of NADPH and DHF, by about 8°C and 31°C, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The m-values for GuHCl denaturation are essentially independent of the concentration of NADPH and have an average value of 1.4 (±0.1) kcal mol−1 M−1.
source: The m-values are essentially independent of the concentration of NADPH and were found to have an average value of 1.4 (±0.1) kcal mol−1 M−1.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The chimera contains an N-terminal His7-tag.
source: The Pet21a plasmid containing the gene for eGFP (with the mutation A206K that stabilizes its monomeric state) and an N-terminal His7-tag (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2017) was amplified by PCR using the following respective forward and reverse primers:
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The eGFP in the chimera contains the mutation A206K that stabilizes its monomeric state.
source: The Pet21a plasmid containing the gene for eGFP (with the mutation A206K that stabilizes its monomeric state) and an N-terminal His7-tag (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2017) was amplified by PCR using the following respective forward and reverse primers:
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A TEV protease cleavage site was introduced at the C-terminus of eGFP.
source: This amplification resulted in introducing a TEV protease cleavage site at the C-terminus of eGFP.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Km of NADPH for DHFRMp is 13 µM.
source: where [S] is the concentration of NADPH and Km is its Michaelis-Menten constant of 13 µM (Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation.
